analysis.one_liner: Caps pain-and-suffering awards in medical malpractice lawsuits at $250,000 and shields FDA-approved drug makers from punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 217-203 on September 26, 2002, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten malpractice rules nationwide. It would have capped compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 no matter how bad the injury, limited the share lawyers can take from a recovery, made punitive damages much harder to win, and barred punitive damages against any drug or device the FDA approved. It would have applied to every state, overriding state rules unless a state's rules were even more protective of doctors and hospitals. The House passed it along party lines; the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and nursing homes facing malpractice insurance premiums, the insurers that write those policies, and drug and device manufacturers would gain the most: lower exposure to large jury awards, hard limits on what injured patients can collect for pain and suffering, and near-immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved products. Supporters argued patients would also benefit through lower health costs and better access to care if malpractice premiums fell.

how_it_helps.text: Keeps recovery of actual economic losses — medical bills, lost wages — fully unlimited, so anyone with real out-of-pocket losses can still recover them in full.

Caps noneconomic damages (pain, suffering, disfigurement, loss of enjoyment of life) at $250,000 per case, no matter how many defendants or claims, which backers said would reduce unpredictable jury awards and lower malpractice insurance premiums.
Limits lawyer contingency fees on a sliding scale (40% of the first $50,000 down to 15% above $600,000), which backers said would leave more of any recovery with the patient.

Bars punitive damages against manufacturers of FDA-approved drugs and devices unless the company knowingly misled the FDA or bribed an FDA official, and shields doctors who prescribed such approved products from product-liability suits.

States findings that the liability system raises health costs and deters information-sharing among providers, framing the caps as a way to reduce defensive medicine and improve patient access to care.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence would bear the cost: the $250,000 cap falls hardest on people whose injuries cause pain and disability but little verifiable economic loss — children, retirees, and stay-at-home parents. Juries would not even be told the cap exists; judges would silently cut awards above it. Punitive-damage limits would also make the worst corporate misconduct harder to punish, and the bill would override more generous state remedies for injured patients.

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on pain and suffering applies regardless of how severe the injury is — a child facing lifelong disability from a birth injury, or a retired person, may have small economic losses and so would collect almost nothing beyond medical bills.
Juries would be barred from being told the cap exists, and any larger award would be quietly reduced by the court, so the people deciding the case would not know their verdict would be cut.

Drug and device makers would be immune from punitive damages for any FDA-approved product unless a patient could prove the company knowingly withheld required information from the FDA or bribed an official — a very high bar for misconduct that injures many people.
The bill would preempt state law nationwide, overriding state remedies that are more generous to injured patients while allowing states to keep only rules that give providers even more protection.

Critics of damage caps argue they give negligent providers and insurers a windfall while doing little to weed out bad doctors, since the same cap applies to gross negligence and to honest error alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The argument for the bill — lower malpractice premiums, less defensive medicine, more predictable awards — is genuine, and economic losses like medical bills and lost wages stay fully recoverable. But the trade is lopsided: the entire benefit to the health system is paid for by the most severely injured patients, who lose most of their compensation precisely because their suffering is great while their paychecks were small. Blanket immunity from punitive damages for FDA-approved products also removes a major private check on drug and device makers, relying entirely on FDA enforcement. The bill's own nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that insurers should be liable for harmful coverage decisions suggests even its sponsors saw a gap it did not fill.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on a mostly party-line 217-203 vote, but the Senate never took it up and it died when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 25, 2002 by Rep. James Greenwood and referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Both committees reported the bill amended on September 25, 2002, and the Rules Committee gave it a closed rule allowing only one hour of debate and no floor amendments.

A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions — a last-chance attempt to send it back to committee for changes — failed 193-225, with 186 of 209 voting Democrats in favor and only 6 of 222 voting Republicans.
The House passed the bill 217-203: 203 of 222 voting Republicans voted yes while 187 of 209 voting Democrats voted no.
The Senate received the bill the same day and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, where it sat without action until the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients kept whatever remedies their state laws allowed, and the plaintiffs' bar kept existing fee structures and damage rules. Doctors, malpractice insurers, and drug makers did not get the federal caps and liability shields they sought, though the House vote showed the issue had a majority coalition in one chamber.

for.name: Rep. James C. Greenwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 25, 2002 and shepherded it through committee and floor passage.

for.name: 203 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage; 115 House Republicans had also cosponsored the bill.

for.name: House Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported a closed rule (H. Res. 553) allowing only one hour of debate and no amendments beyond a motion to recommit, which the House adopted.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on September 26, 2002 and never reported it or scheduled a vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: 187 of 208 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; 186 of them had also backed the motion to recommit with instructions.

against.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to both committees, a motion that failed 193-225.

against.name: 15 of 223 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, joining most Democrats in opposition.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 203 of 222 voting Republicans yes versus 15 no, and 14 of 209 voting Democrats yes versus 187 no; the one Independent voted no. The failed motion to recommit was nearly the mirror image — 186 Democrats yes, 6 Republicans.

industries.note: Hard caps on pain-and-suffering awards and punitive damages would directly shrink the claims these insurers pay out, lowering premiums for their doctor customers at the cost of the largest awards to the most badly injured patients.

The bill would bar punitive damages for any FDA-approved product and shield prescribing doctors from product-liability suits, leaving FDA enforcement as the main private-side check on unsafe drugs and devices.

Providers would gain capped liability and lower malpractice premiums, which backers said would cut defensive medicine and improve access; the cost falls on their injured patients, whose compensation would be capped regardless of fault's severity.
Sliding-scale fee caps and lower damage awards would cut the contingency fees that fund malpractice cases; their financial interest here runs alongside their clients' ability to bring and win cases.

The bill includes a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that insurers should be liable for harm caused by their decisions about medically necessary care, but attaches no legal requirement — a gesture without force.
